detail.abstract: We develop a low-dimensional ecological macroeconomic model with an internally consistent current-flow closure. Environmental quality affects effective productive capacity and evolves endogenously through natural regeneration, production-induced degradation and public remediation.The key feature of the model is an ecological threshold:above a critical level of environmental quality, production is unconstrained; below it, environmental degradation progressively reduces effective output. Substituting the macroeconomic and fiscal relations into the environmental law of motion yields a one-dimensional piecewise-linear map. This tractable structure allows us to characterizesteady states, admissibility conditions, local stability and policy thresholds analytically.We show that ecological thresholds can generate endogenous regime switching between healthy and degraded regimes. Under suitable parameter configurations, the model also produces ecological stop-and-go dynamics, in which phases of unconstrained production and environmental degradation alternate with phases of constrained output and environmental recovery. By explicitly distinguishing between the ecological threshold E_crit and the policy threshold alpha∗, the paper provides a formal link between ecological discontinuities and policy design.The model is not intended to replace richer high-dimensional ecological macroeconomic frameworks, such as ecological SFC models, but to complement them by isolating a basic mechanism in a tractable analytical setting. In this sense, its low dimensionality isa methodological advantage: it makes explicit the threshold, stability and regime-selection conditions that may be harder to identify in simulation-oriented models. Environmental fiscal policy affects both environmental quality and macroeconomic stability.

detail.abstract: Robust capacity planning guards against worst-case technology costs, but its fixed uncertainty set charges every future unit of renewable capacity the same premium, however much a country has already built. We develop a decision-dependent robust goal programming model in which the local component of capital-cost uncertainty is modelled to contract as domestic deployment grows, while global cost uncertainty, which a price-taking country cannot influence, stays fixed. The local width is calibrated from Bangladesh levelised-cost data, net of the global cost spread in the US National Renewable Energy Laboratory’s Annual Technology Baseline, and the demand uncertainty from back-cast errors of the planner’s forecasting rule. Five goals (investment budget, renewable capacity, system cost, emissions and renewable generation) are balanced with an extended Chebyshev achievement function, and the model is reformulated exactly as a mixed-integer linear program. Applied to Bangladesh for 2021-2041, static robustness at the highest protection level considered cuts 2041 solar capacity from 35.4 to 26.1 gigawatts and adds 64 million tonnes of carbon dioxide. Allowing decision-dependence recovers up to 1.7 gigawatts, worth 1.1-4.8% of the goal-achievement objective across learning strengths; this value vanishes when build limits fix the deployment pace. In a rolling back-test from 2020, protecting reliability one to two years ahead removed the observed shortfall at an additional modelled cost of 1.3 billion US dollars, against 16-21 billion for full-horizon protection. A 40% renewable-capacity pathway analysed by the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis is met in every plan, but renewables reach only 20-24% of generation.

detail.abstract: Digital technologies are increasingly recognised as strategic instruments for advancing corporate decarbonisation. However, there is limited understanding of whether such technologies foster firms' willingness to pursue low-carbon transformation prior to the implementation of concrete actions. Drawing on data from Chinese A-share listed manufacturing firms spanning 2010 to 2023, this paper examines the effect of digital technology adoption on the propensity for low-carbon transformation, as measured through text analysis of corporate social responsibility reports. The degree of digital technology adoption is assessed via large-language-model-based semantic analysis of annual reports. The findings reveal that digital technology significantly enhances manufacturing firms' willingness to undertake low-carbon transformation. This effect remains robust after accounting for high-dimensional fixed effects, annual report textual tone and length, alternative measures of digital technology, double machine learning, and instrumental variable approaches. Mechanism tests indicate that digital technology operates primarily by reducing the costs associated with carbon emissions abatement and by strengthening firms’ commitment to environmental responsibility. Heterogeneity tests further demonstrate that this effect is more pronounced among state-owned enterprises and in non-heavy-polluting industries. Further analysis reveals that environmental attention, from government and the public, along with direct and indirect environmental subsidies, reinforces the positive effect of digital technology. These results contribute to the literature of business strategy and environmental management, demonstrating that digital technology is a strategic capability connecting environmental responsibility, economic feasibility, and corporate readiness to engage in low-carbon transformation.

detail.abstract: Reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from agriculture is essential for meeting climate targets. Although market-based policy instruments for reducing GHG emissions, such as emissions taxes, could be effective, they remain politically sensitive. A central concern is that these taxes reduce the income of taxed farms and could increase income inequality among farmers. However, GHG taxes also generate public revenues that can be redistributed to farmers. The design of this redistribution determines the extent to which income losses are compensated and can increase or reduce the effects of the tax on income inequality. This paper provides an ex ante assessment of alternative tax revenue redistribution schemes and examines how they affect the environmental effectiveness and fairness aspects of GHG taxes in agriculture. Using a national-scale agent-based model for Swiss agriculture, we compare a GHG emissions tax combined with three alternative redistribution schemes: a uniform per-hectare lump-sum rebate, a compensation of costs for technical mitigation measures, and a compensation according to the abatement potential of the adopted technical mitigation measures. We evaluate these redistribution schemes using indicators capturing fairness and effectiveness and compliance with the polluter-pays principle. The results show that while a lump-sum rebate improves several fairness-related indicators, it weakens environmental effectiveness by favoring larger, more polluting farms. By contrast, mitigation-based distribution schemes enhance both fairness overall and effectiveness, with compensation for technical mitigation costs achieving the largest additional emissions reduction. These findings highlight the importance of redistribution design for an effective and fair agricultural climate policy to further reduce emissions.

detail.abstract: Policymakers are increasingly turning to drinking water system consolidation to address per-sistent water quality and compliance challenges in under-resourced communities. Consolidation is a common strategy for capturing economies of scale across industries, yet evidence on how it affects quality is limited. I estimate the effects of drinking water system consolidation in California using a staggered difference-in-differences design, focusing on outcomes consumers directly experience: regulatory violations, contaminant concentrations, and monthly bills. Consolidation reduces total Safe Drinking Water Act violations by 64%, with declines in health-based and monitoring and reporting violations and in indices of contaminant concentrations. These pooled effects mask substantial heterogeneity: among systems designated as failing before consolidation, consolidation leads to approximately 1.24 (48%) fewer total violations per year, with little change in monthly bills. Consolidations involving systems without prior compliance struggles show little change in violations but suggestive evidence of lower bills. Receiving systems experience no statistically significant increase in operating expenses. Overall, the results suggest that consolidation can improve drinking water quality for communities served by struggling systems without imposing substantial costs on the systems that receive them.

detail.title: Long-Run Economic Impacts of Climate Variability
detail.abstract: We estimate long-run economic impacts of climate variability by employing a stochastic frontier model where climate variability is additionally included into the production frontier. Our climate panel dataset covers 157 countries over the period 1950-2014. We find that both temperature and precipitation affect production possibilities in a hump-shaped way. Most importantly, temperature variability turns out to reduce long-term potential output. This negative effect is found to be statistically significant, and various robustness checks, including income as well as temperature heterogeneity across nations, confirm it. We also find short-term weather anomalies, either temperature or precipitation, are statistically insignificant in most specifications. Our findings provide supporting empirical evidence for a growing body of Integrated Assessment Model literature, emphasizing the role of uncertainty about global temperature dynamics.

detail.abstract: Objective To identify determinants of child wasting and examine its spatial distribution across Thailand using multilevel analysis integrated with validated spatial interpolation. Design Secondary data analysis from the 6th Thailand Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS6). We applied multilevel logistic regression to identify factors associated with wasting, and interpolated province-level coefficients from the final model to estimate spatial patterns. We assessed the predictive performance via leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV). The setting is 12 provinces: 6 provinces in the southern border region of Thailand and 6 socioeconomically disadvantaged provinces in the rest of the regions. The sample size for this study were 4,998 children aged 0-59 months. Results The wasting prevalence was 9.2% which was higher than the national estimate and there was large variation geographically. Children in Songkhla and Nakhon Ratchasima were more likely to be wasted than children in Bangkok. The risk was also increased in infants aged 0–5 months and in children living in urban areas. At the community level, there was still a substantial variation (ICC = 17.34%) which indicated a significant contextual effect on child wasting. Spatial interpolation identified clusters of high risk of wasting in the NorthEast, lower Central region and Southern border provinces. Validation however showed limited predictive accuracy suggesting that the interpolated map should be considered an exploratory representation of spatial heterogeneity and not a precise predictive tool. Conclusions Child wasting in Thailand remains unevenly distributed among provinces, and is influenced by individual and community level factors. The combination of multilevel modelling and spatial analysis provides useful evidence to identify geographic disparities and to target nutrition interventions. Nevertheless, the modest predictive accuracy observed in this study points out the necessity of validating spatial interpolation models before their use in public health decision making.

detail.abstract:
As students increasingly rely on GenAI platforms to generate code and build models, educators face a new challenge: identifying and nurturing the analytical skills that remain relevant in an increasingly AI-enabled society. This case study explores this challenge through a supervised classification exercise. MBA students used GenAI to develop Machine Learning models based on Decision Trees, Random Forests, Naive Bayes, and Logistic Regression. A guided assignment was conducted in two phases. In the first stage, students were directed to “ask GenAI to perform the analyses”.

However, the standard procedure of GenAI agents is to deploy label encoding unless directed otherwise. This representational choice would become a focal point during the second phase, when students were instructed to use a semantic encoding approach.  A major turning point occurred when students were asked to explain results obtained from the label-encoded dataset versus the semantically encoded dataset. That comparison revealed that semantic encoding (that is, enacted or supervised by a human) generated distinct effects on predictive performance while substantially improving interpretability.

The case enables educators to shift classroom discussion away from computational execution and toward assessing the meaning of variables and models. Important lessons emerged from the exercise, which can be used to further explore and extend the exercise. The most relevant lesson is that using GenAI in a curated way does not replace analytical thinking but rather relocates it toward higher-order forms of reasoning.

detail.abstract: On two-sided platforms that match users with independent providers, demand concentrates on a few providers who may later decline requests, causing failed matching attempts. Physician-patient matching on online health consultation (OHC) platforms suffers from this exact problem. While OHC platforms encourage teams to increase capacity, the capacity teams create does not, on its own, translate into matching. The platform cannot assign a request or observe whether a displayed provider or team has capacity or interest, so its feasible instrument is the menu it presents, including which providers appear, in what order, and with what information. Building on large language model (LLM) agents, we propose a menu-intervention design listing provider teams and an evaluation framework to test the design. In the design, a triage agent reads free text that a department-level rule cannot, a provider agent simulates each candidate's accept-or-decline reply, and a ranking agent orders the menu on those replies. In the evaluation, empirically grounded LLM agents stand in for patients and capacity-constrained providers, so that the same request is replayed under alternative designs that no live platform can test. Using data from haodf.com, a leading OHC platform in China, we show that the menu intervention can reduce the failure rate, the ratio of requests ending with no consultation delivered, from 65.9% to 37.4% by listing teams. Teams accept more requests than solo physicians, and the menu converts that capacity into delivered consultations. Replacing department-level rules with the LLM at triage and ranking decreases the failure rate further to 27.5%. Intervening only after a decline and disclosing each candidate's accept-or-decline reply lower it to 12.1%. Platforms gain more by revealing information they already hold than by selecting candidates more cleverly.

detail.abstract:
AI governance requires more than policies, model safeguards and audit logs operating separately. Institutional requirements must remain connected to the actions AI systems perform, the evidence of their consequences, and procedures for intervention and remedy. This paper proposes an Integrated AI Governance and Safety Architecture (IAGSA), a vendor-neutral reference architecture spanning ten functional domains. Its contributions include an integrated responsibility model, explicit authority–effect–evidence contracts, six acceptance gates, 25 research requirements and an executable research demonstrator.

Evaluation combines managed-cloud witness signing and storage, policy engines, operating-system identity separation, model-driven tool use and organizational failure and recovery workflows. The combined protocol matched predeclared expectations across 24 scenarios, including deliberately exposed controls that produced prohibited effects. A separate classifier experiment released 38 incorrect classifications among 285 synthetic workflow outputs; all 38 were subsequently corrected through scripted procedures.

These findings demonstrate the feasibility of the tested technical composition while identifying consequential failure boundaries. Valid authorization does not establish decision correctness, and a denial on one route does not prevent effects through an exposed alternative. Governance therefore requires evaluating authorization, substantive decision quality, effect enforcement, evidence integrity and remedy together.

The proposal and accompanying technical package support inspection, reproduction and further development. Results concern the configurations and conditions tested; institutional legitimacy, real human oversight, independent administrative custody and representative production effectiveness require separate evaluation.

detail.abstract: We examine how user-generated short-form video attention maps onto the local business consumer journey. Using monthly panel data on 7,480 local businesses from Naver Place, a nationwide digital platform in Korea, we link short-form video (clip) plays and uploads to five observable stages: page views, unique visitors, saves, direction clicks, and bookings. Clip attention is positively related to all five stages, but the association weakens along the funnel and is far smaller for direction clicks and bookings than for page views. To capture this asymmetry, we construct an Attention–Action Gap Index measuring how far page views outpace direction clicks and bookings, and find that the gap widens with both clip plays and clip uploads. For low-visibility businesses, clip attention is associated with larger gains in page views, while the gap widens rather than narrows. Bookings, by contrast, measured only where a platform reservation function is enabled, show that clip attention is significantly associated with completed reservations within that subsample. Thus, we find that short-form video is closely tied to discovery and consideration, while its association weakens sharply at the step to action. By locating where attention stops translating into action, our study shows that the value of user-generated short-form video for local businesses cannot be inferred from views or plays alone.

detail.abstract: Few studies report how large language models (LLMs) perform in the day-to-day operations of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) on primary data, including cost and latency. We examine human-approved AI classification of 1,042 invoice line items of a Hungarian SME, retrieved from the Online Invoice system of the Hungarian Tax and Customs Administration (NAV), into company-specific managerial allocation categories. The sample was deliberately chosen so that the manager’s original labeling contained errors (81 items, 7.8%); all results are measured against the reviewed reference. We compared eight models from four providers (one low-cost and one mid-tier, reasoning-capable model each) with three category-description prompts, and then ran the low-cost models with a partner and item list built from the reviewed labels of the same 1,042 items (learned context). A detailed description written jointly by the manager and an AI raised mean accuracy across the eight models from 83.2% to 91.4% compared with the plain description. The mid-tier models added at most 2.7 percentage points at 4.7 to 17.9 times the cost and with longer response times. With learned context, the low-cost models reached 97.1–99.9% accuracy on this dataset, typically below USD 0.5 per 1,000 items, exceeding the 92.2% accuracy of the original production labeling; because the context was built from the same items, this is an upper-bound estimate for a known set of business partners, not accuracy validated on new invoices. With descriptions derived from error-containing data, the models repeated 16.4% of the human errors; conversely, reviewing the 8.8% of items on which the models disagreed with the human label caught 79% of the errors. For SMEs, company-specific context and verified training data matter more than model size.

title: Predictive Modeling of Customer Churn Using Customer Engagement Metrics in E-commerce
affiliations: University of Sri Jayewardenepura

detail.title: Predictive Modeling of Customer Churn Using Customer Engagement Metrics in E-commerce
detail.abstract: Customer churn is a significant challenge in the e-commerce industry, where retaining existing customers requires a clear understanding of customer engagement and behavioral patterns. This study investigates the use of machine learning techniques to analyze customer churn using six customer-related behavioral features: age, total purchases, login frequency, average session duration, discount usage rate, and customer service calls. A dataset containing 50,000 customer records was analyzed through an integrated framework combining unsupervised customer segmentation and supervised churn prediction. K-Means clustering was applied after data preprocessing and feature standardization, with the Elbow Method and Silhouette Score used to determine the appropriate number of clusters. Two customer segments were identified, with observed churn rates of 18.67% and 35.19%, indicating meaningful differences in customer engagement and churn behavior. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was further used to visualize the identified segments. For churn prediction, Logistic Regression was employed as an interpretable baseline and compared with Random Forest models using the same six core features. A further Random Forest model incorporating the customer segment was evaluated to determine whether segmentation improved predictive performance. The Random Forest model incorporating customer segment achieved the best performance, with an accuracy of 78.55%, precision of 67.65%, recall of 49.41%, F1-score of 57.11%, and ROC-AUC of 0.8165. Five-fold stratified cross-validation also demonstrated stronger discrimination for Random Forest than Logistic Regression. The findings indicate that customer engagement metrics provide useful signals for churn analysis and that combining behavioral segmentation with predictive modeling can support more informed customer retention strategies in e-commerce.

detail.abstract: Enterprise AI governance typically begins with allocating decision rights: routine tasks to the machine, high-stakes judgment to humans, with a person “in the loop” to review outputs. This paper argues that classifying who holds a decision does nothing, on its own, to ensure that person retains the standing capacity to make it well. Drawing on Microsoft’s Copilot deployment and Klarna’s AI customer-service reversal, we identify four mechanisms through which human judgment erodes beneath intact formal authority: deskilling through lost repetition, miscalibrated trust, diffused accountability, and erosion of employee self-trust. We introduce the “judgment layer”: the habits, skills, information, incentives, and feedback loops that determine whether the person assigned a decision can still exercise it well. Assembling established human-oversight research into a single practical instrument, we propose a four-pillar diagnostic (repetition and practice; epistemic access and error detection; causal power and override friction; accountable ownership and learning loops) that leaders can use to assess whether the human capability beneath a decision right is being preserved. The central claim: we do not need humans in the AI’s loop. We need AI in the human’s loop.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how the 2025-2026 AI policy directions of Japan, the European Union and the United States shape opportunities for advanced agentic AI. A structured documentary analysis codes 17 policy units against six common questions concerning activities, instruments, responsible actors, complementary assets, risk allocation and potential economic returns. The corpus covers measures in place or announced by 22 October 2026; an appendix records source roles, coding decisions and evidence locations. Three comparative findings emerge. All three cases combine promotion with risk management, making a simple regulation-versus-innovation divide inadequate. Their implementation channels differ: Japan connects national coordination to domain deployment; the EU combines differentiated market obligations with shared adoption infrastructure; and the USA combines federal expansion measures with security initiatives and state-level duties. Across the cases, access to data, evaluation and organisational capacity recurs as a link between model capability and deployment. A four-component economic framework-capability, complementary assets, verification and accountability-connects these documentary findings to sectoral testbeds and business models. A hypothetical cost illustration includes residual losses in both the baseline and AI process; its results show how verification costs can reverse net gains at a given deployment volume. Five hypotheses specify subsequent empirical tests. The findings concern selected policy configurations and intended mechanisms, without identifying causal effects on productivity. The contribution is an auditable comparison showing how different allocations of implementation and verification responsibilities create distinct, overlapping opportunities for AI services.

detail.abstract: Research on cryptocurrency in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) has focused on formal regulation, on the permissibility of crypto-assets under Islamic law, and on individual investment intentions. Less is known about how foreign digital-asset ventures and Gulf investors and regulators negotiate acceptance in practice. This paper asks how unwritten institutional and cultural codes shaped the reception of a foreign crypto-mining venture in the Gulf. Drawing on economic anthropology and institutional theory, it uses analytic autoethnography: the author, who led the regional business of a Dubai - headquartered mining firm in 2021–2023, re-examines a commercial presentation she wrote, which a colleague delivered at an industry summit in 2022. The analysis identifies four codes: formal permission that did not amount to acceptance; Sharia compliance located in the form of the contract rather than the nature of the product; country of origin as a liability that varied by audience; and energy as a public resource requiring justification. The paper argues that the venture's main deficit lay in its knowledge of its counterparts' institutions, not in investors' knowledge of mining. Comparing the 2022 claims with developments up to 2026, including Oman's state-mandated mining pool, it shows that the region did become a mining hub, but on terms set by Gulf states and investors. It then raises an open question: as Islamic finance moves into crypto-assets, a sector where much capital moves through opaque channels, will Sharia governance accommodate those channels or act as a brake on them? The mechanisms identified are not specific to crypto-mining and may apply to foreign technology ventures more broadly, including AI and data-centre infrastructure. The paper offers four propositions for comparative research. Findings are drawn from a single case and are presented as analytical, not statistical, generalisations.

detail.abstract: Consumer privacy regulation rests on two propositions: that platforms may use consumer data in ways that harm consumers or competition, and that limiting the amount of data collected will curb such conduct. Using a two-year field experiment at Wayfair, we find the opposite on the first point-personalization actually improves consumerproduct match quality: personalized consumers are 4.4% less likely to return purchases and 2.1% to 3.2% more likely to repurchase within a year. These gains do not come from steering consumers toward higher-margin products; instead, the platform benefits through repeat purchases, while small sellers gain visibility and sales relative to large sellers. Combining the platform's personalization algorithm with a structural model, we then show that privacy restrictions such as Safari's 7-day cookie policy would reduce consumer welfare by 13.1%. Yet the rule offers incomplete privacy protection: the algorithm can infer mainstream consumers' preferences from similar peers, and niche consumers' preferences from their own distinctive surviving data. The largest losses fall on consumers in the middle, for whom neither channel is strong. Such restrictions may therefore fail to protect consumers, for two reasons: (i) positive data externalities that recover mainstream preferences, and (ii) own-signal precision, whereby some consumers' data is distinctive enough to identify them even without externalities. An effective privacy policy should target algorithmic inference itself, not merely the amount of data these algorithms use.

detail.abstract: Debates about generative AI and misinformation usually start from content: what is false, who spreads it and how platforms should respond. This article starts from price. It argues that the costs AI's price leaves out link the labour-market effects of AI to the degradation of the information environment. Three costs are largely missing from the price of AI output: producing and replenishing the human knowledge models learn from, checking what they produce, and the errors that remain, which fall on whoever relies on them. Drawing on an integrative review of peer-reviewed studies, official statistics and independent audits from 2023 to 2026, with Australia as a case, the article traces four mechanisms through which these unpriced costs become information disorder: correlated error at scale, recursive depletion of public knowledge, the collapse of the referral bargain that funded original reporting, and adversarial seeding of the material models read. Together they produce a commons that is fragmented and homogenised at once and, for countries that import their AI, a strategic dependence. The central claim is that an input that is unpriced is also unguarded: the features that make AI output cheap make the information supply cheap to pollute and expensive to defend. The article compares how the United States, China and the European Union assign these costs, derives six propositions for empirical research, and argues that measuring the health of the information supply offers a route to policy that does not require governments to adjudicate truth.

detail.abstract: Introduction: Patients receiving medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD) may require subacute rehabilitation (SAR) after hospitalization, yet facility policies and medication logistics can delay or prevent placement. Responses were classified as unqualified yes, conditional, no, or unavailable. Follow-up questions addressed prescribing, pharmacy access, OTP relationships, transportation, weekend coverage, payer requirements, and reasons for declination. Facility-specific conditions related to prescribing, OTP coordination, transportation, payer requirements, and disposition identified actionable targets for improving post-acute MOUD access.

detail.abstract: Behavioural-health data can help public institutions understand community needs, evaluate services, and design more responsive policies. These data may originate in clinical care, social services, surveys, community organizations, and digital platforms, and can reveal highly sensitive information about distress, substance use, relationships, and daily routines. Their reuse creates a governance challenge: public value must be pursued without normalizing excessive surveillance, discriminatory profiling, or secondary uses that affected communities could not reasonably anticipate. This conceptual review examines ethical governance, privacy protection, accountability, and responsible analytics in behavioural-health policymaking. It draws on contemporary literature on healthcare AI ethics, data privacy, and international guidance, and incorporates Akinyelure's (2025) argument that community insights should be connected to policy decisions through institutional capacity and ethical data governance. The paper proposes a lifecycle framework covering purpose legitimacy, data minimization, protection and impact assessment, responsible analysis, and accountable use. It emphasizes that de-identification alone cannot eliminate re-identification risk, consent may be difficult in public-sector contexts, and algorithmic fairness requires attention to structural inequalities in the data-generating process. The framework recommends independent oversight, transparent public communication, limits on onward sharing, meaningful avenues for contesting decisions, and periodic review of whether data use remains necessary and proportionate. No new empirical data or experimental results are presented. The paper concludes that responsible behavioural-health data policy depends less on a single privacy technology than on enforceable institutional practices, community participation, and clear accountability for harms.

detail.abstract: Background & Objective: Independent high-density food and beverage micro-retailers face severe operational compression from two opposing forces: high thermal-energy overhead coupled with rapid inventory decay in perishable categories (fresh produce, frozen animal proteins, and frozen confectionery), and intense price competition in shelf-stable functional beverages (hydration and caffeinated energy drinks). This study presents a quantitative operational framework that integrates cold-chain inventory modeling, cross-category price elasticity, and ergonomic spatial planogramming to maximize gross revenue per square meter (R_sqm) and net operating margin. Methods: Over a 12-month longitudinal operating cycle in a high-traffic urban retail enterprise in Vladivostok, inventory turnover, spoilage waste (W_i), gross margin return on inventory investment (GMROII), and basket co-occurrence probabilities were tracked across five core stock-keeping unit (SKU) verticals: (1) Frozen Animal Proteins (meat and pelagic/demersal fish), (2) Fresh Produce (high-perishability fruits), (3) Frozen Confectionery (ice cream), (4) Functional & Caffeinated Beverages (energy drinks), and (5) Staple Hydration (bottled water). We formulated a modified Economic Order Quantity model for decaying goods (EOQ_d) paired with an eye-tracking-informed spatial planogram based on human visual ergonomics. Results: Implementation of the quantitative replenishment and spatial merchandising architecture generated $700,000+ USD equivalent in annual gross revenue, reduced perishable fruit shrinkage from 11.4% to 3.8%, and elevated overall store GMROII by 34.2%. Cross-category basket analysis revealed a high synergistic attachment rate (P(B|A) = 0.64) between functional energy beverages and staple protein/produce purchases when cold-vault planograms were arranged along primary customer kinetic pathways. Conclusions: Treating small-footprint perishable retail as a mathematical flow-and-thermodynamics system allows independent operators to achieve institutional-grade inventory efficiency and high gross turnover without expanding physical floor space.

detail.abstract:
This research monograph develops and empirically examines a multidimensional framework for evaluating economic achievement based on the Philosophy of Belonging.

Conventional measures of economic performance emphasize income per capita, growth, inequality, and human development. However, these indicators do not necessarily capture the institutional and relational conditions that enable individuals to participate effectively in economic and social life.

Using a sample of 55 countries, the study examines four indicators of belonging: institutional access, perceived care from neighbors, perceived care from government, and reported discrimination.

These indicators are analyzed in relation to national income, the World Bank Gini index, the United Nations Development Programme’s Human Development Index, economic growth, and macroeconomic growth volatility.

The empirical analysis employs cross-country correlations and ordinary least squares regressions with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors.

The results reveal important differences between conventional economic indicators and the institutional and relational dimensions of belonging. Institutional access is strongly associated with income and human development, whereas perceived care follows different patterns. Income inequality is negatively associated with perceived care from neighbors and government, including after controlling for national income.

The analysis also demonstrates the importance of considering freedom of expression when interpreting reported discrimination.

Finally, economic growth, stability, income distribution, and human capabilities are shown to represent empirically distinct dimensions of economic achievement.

The findings suggest that economic performance should be evaluated through a multidimensional framework that incorporates material prosperity, distribution, institutional participation, social recognition, and human capabilities.

The study contributes to development economics, welfare economics, and political economy by providing an empirical foundation for the Economics of Belonging.

detail.abstract: India's Right to Education Rules guarantee a primary school within one kilometre and an upper-primary school within three, measured as walking distance. Nobody measures it. Using geotagged coordinates from India's Unified District Information System for Education (UDISE+) and a complete five-year census of Karnataka's 74,309 schools (371,545 report cards), we make the measurement. 455 rural government school records ceased in 2025-26, a closure rate of 1.110% that had doubled a year before the programme is usually dated. To the nearest surviving school teaching the displaced pupils' grades, 51.3% of closures keep primary pupils within one kilometre in straight-line distance but only 28.1% by road; for classes VI-VII, 93.6% and 67.3% are within three kilometres. Walking routes are 1.344 times the straight line. The choice of metric moves primary compliance by twenty-three points; requiring a grade-capable destination moves it by two. The binding constraint is the one-kilometre primary norm: networks small enough to be called consolidation leave primary compliance at 23-37% by road, and a network meeting the primary and upper-primary norms in straight-line distance needs about 27,300 sites. detail.abstract: Cryptocurrency prices often swing by double digits in a single day, and these moves frequently follow a viral post, a trending hashtag or a wave of fear on online forums rather than any change in fundamentals. This paper examines how investor behaviour shapes crypto market volatility, focusing on three linked forces: social media, herding and market sentiment. Through a structured narrative review of twenty studies from behavioural finance and the crypto literature, it builds a framework that traces how online information becomes attention, how attention turns into sentiment, and how herding converts sentiment into trading pressure and volatility. The review finds strong evidence that search interest, social media activity and posts by prominent figures predict trading volume and short term price moves. Herding is present in crypto markets, grows stronger in extreme conditions, and helps explain bubbles and sudden crashes. Retail investors, many of them young and new to investing, are central to these dynamics, and they tend to chase past gains in crypto even when they behave more cautiously in stocks. Manipulation, from coordinated promotion to suspicious trading and timed stablecoin issuance, exploits these same behavioural patterns. The paper discusses implications for investors, platforms and regulators, including the need for better disclosure by influencers, stronger action against coordinated manipulation, and investor education that addresses behavioural biases directly, with attention to young crypto communities in markets such as Nigeria.

detail.abstract: Firm-level research on government demand needs two things that raw public procurement records do not supply: the date on which a contract became public, and the listed company that held the contracting entity on that date. Hall's (1978) insight, central to the 2026 Prize in Economic Sciences, is that forward-looking agents respond only to new information, so the date information arrives defines the shock. We describe a point-in-time, entity-resolved dataset of U.S. federal contract actions and related disclosure records (850,000+ resolved events as of October 2026) built for this purpose. Each record carries its activity date, its publication date with statutory lags applied, and a ticker that traded on the publication date. We document three construction errors that affect naive joins and measure what correcting them changes: activity-date dating places defense contract information 90 days early, a current-parent join misattributes 3.3% of resolved contract dollars, and daily announcements reveal 93.5% of matched defense awards a median 90 days before the award record. Ten record types pass accuracy checks against original public documents at 95% or better. We report no return or performance results.

detail.abstract: In the context of climate change and the well-established links between personality traits and life outcomes, this paper presents a novel investigation into the causal effects of natural disaster-induced housing damage on the Big Five personality traits. Using a time-varying, plausibly exogenous measure of local cyclone exposure as an instrument within an individual fixed effects instrumental variable framework, we find that weather-related home damage significantly reduces Conscientiousness and Emotional Stability, while increasing Openness to Experience. These effects are highly heterogeneous: significant impacts emerge only in quantile regression models, with individuals at the lower end of the Conscientiousness and Emotional Stability distributions more adversely affected, and those at the upper end of the Openness distribution exhibiting greater increases. Furthermore, our findings suggest that weather-related home damage may indirectly reduce earnings by altering personality traits in ways associated with lower income—effects that are not only statistically significant but also substantial in magnitude and economically meaningful. These personality changes may correspond to income losses of up to 7%, with socioeconomically disadvantaged individuals being most severely affected. We also identify heterogeneous impacts of home damage by gender and age, varying by trait and across the distribution of each trait.

detail.abstract: When an agent chooses for a person, the person consumes what the agent chose, and the agent learns from what it executed. This paper develops the third component of the Theory of Delegated Markets, recursive demand: the claim that repeated delegation moves people's later preferences, willingness to pay, and independent decision capability toward the consumption pathways their agents selected. I define the three outcomes as measurable properties, each read outside the agent's interface, and three moderators (autonomy of execution, exposure diversity, and the implicit share of feedback) as audited properties of the architecture, and state five boundary conditions as premises. A stylized model yields one closed form, the absorption share: the fraction of an agent's interpretive offset that ends in the principal's own preference. It equals one when an autonomous agent learns only from its own executions, because the representation is then never corrected and the person moves to it, and it exceeds one when the agent reads its own executions as evidence that she wants more of them. A decomposition separates exposure, execution, and evidence-loop components. Eight propositions, RD1 to RD8, follow, each with a mechanism, a boundary, and a falsifier. Three designs are specified, none of them run for this paper: a controlled agent simulation, the pre-registered Proof-Based Pricing run as a zerorecursion template, and a pre-registered longitudinal experiment. The construct fails if principals with matched baselines, assigned to agents applying different defensible interpretations of one mandate, show no systematic divergence in independently measured later preferences.

detail.abstract:
In IKEA v. Vlaams Belang, the CJEU addressed, for the first time, the conflict between trade mark rights and political freedom of expression. This commentary examines the judgment’s significance, its shortcomings and the questions it leaves unresolved.

The Court’s express recognition that political parody may justify the unauthorised use of a reputed trade mark, even where the political message is unrelated to the mark or its proprietor, is a welcome development. Yet the commentary questions whether the Court’s approach offers meaningful protection for such expression in practice. It examines the uncertainties surrounding the requirement of good faith and the speaker’s intentions, as well as the potentially circular reasoning that allows reputation, similarity and the advantage gained from using a famous mark to count against the speaker, even though these same characteristics may be essential to the political message. It also considers the Court’s treatment of the mark’s cultural significance, the distinction between political and commercial expression, and the apparent inconsistency with its copyright case law concerning expressive uses and users’ rights.

More fundamentally, the commentary argues that the Court approaches the conflict predominantly through the economic logic of trade mark law, without adequately explaining how restrictions on political expression satisfy the strict necessity standard under Article 10 ECHR. A closer examination of the Court’s own observations on the IKEA-Plan reveals further tensions, particularly concerning the campaign’s use of IKEA as a cultural reference and the risk of implying political endorsement. The commentary concludes that, despite its welcome recognition of political parody, the judgment risks making political expression accommodate the demands of trade mark protection, rather than requiring trade mark law to accommodate freedom of expression.

detail.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into environmental governance is essential for shifting from reactive compliance to proactive ecological protection. Despite India’s constitutional mandate for environmental justice, structural enforcement deficits render traditional regulatory mechanisms inadequate. While emerging predictive technologies offer promising results for anticipatory pollution control, a critical research gap exists regarding algorithmic accountability and the doctrinal vacancy surrounding criminal liability for AI-mediated environmental offences. This paper proposes the doctrinal foundations for an algorithmic accountability framework to address the liability gap created when autonomous systems generate environmental harm. Employing a doctrinal and comparative legal methodology, the study analyses constitutional principles, existing statutes, and judicial precedents. Results indicate that current anthropocentric criminal laws structurally insulate corporate entities from liability for algorithmic negligence. The findings suggest extending absolute liability to corporate algorithmic deployments. The implications underscore the urgent need to amend statutes and mandate independent algorithmic impact assessments to ensure ecological accountability.

detail.abstract: Patient portals have expanded access to outpatient care, but they also create asynchronous communication queues where patient-initiated requests for medical advice may remain unanswered while patients continue making decisions about seeking care. We examine whether unresolved medical-advice requests are associated with subsequent emergency department use, suggesting that delays in responding through patient portals may spill over into acute care. Using 34 months of patient portal and electronic health records data from a large U.S. health system, we analyze 420,517 patient-initiated medical-advice threads spanning 2.93 million thread-days. To capture differences in incoming requests, we use large language models to classify the severity and complexity of each initial patient message. Daily hazard models show that unresolved requests are associated with a higher likelihood of an emergency department visit. After addressing the nonrandom timing of clinician responses using a control-function approach based on workload variation, the estimated effect increases to 1.33 percentage points, suggesting that conventional estimates understate the relationship because higher-risk requests tend to receive faster attention. Emergency department use is concentrated among a small subset of requests. Although high-severity messages account for only 5.4% of medical-advice threads, they represent 28.5% of threads followed by an emergency department visit. Together, these findings show that delays in responding to asynchronous patient messages can have important downstream consequences and that the content of incoming requests-not just their volume-should guide how health systems prioritize limited response capacity.

detail.abstract:
This is the Introduction to Sustainability Essentials: A Leadership Guide for Lawyers (ABA Press, John C. Dernbach, Matthew Bogoshian, & Irma Russell, 2022).

Sustainability Essentials is a short (126 page) practice guide to help anyone in the legal profession find more and better on-ramps to engage in sustainable development in their particular law practices and communities. It is for lawyers at any stage of their career, and it is not limited to environmental law, energy law, or any other specific practice area.

As the Introduction explains, this book is based on two premises. First, there is overwhelming evidence we are not meeting the challenges and opportunities facing our profession, our nation, and the world. Second, while many lawyers are already doing this work, more lawyers need to play a significant role in helping achieve better and more innovative outcomes for their clients and communities, and to accelerate the transition to a sustainable society.

As the Introduction also explains, the book is divided in two broad parts that together provide an on-ramp for this work. The first four chapters of this guide explain the foundation for the use of sustainable development in law practice. Chapter 1 provides an overview of the history of the sustainable development framework, emphasizing the centrality of integrated decision making. Chapter 2 describes in more detail the basic principles lawyers need to know before applying sustainable development in law practice. Chapter 3 explains the lawyer’s ethical duty to clients and society to apply sustainability. It focuses on three fundamental principles of lawyering: compliance with and respect for the law, serving legitimate client interests, and advancing legal reform to serve the public good. In chapter 4, we explain in detail how to apply the sustainable development framework in law practice.

The remaining chapters build on this foundation. Chapter 5 shows how to get started on sustainability leadership in the law. Chapter 6 explains the dynamics of attorney-client conversations about sustainable development, and Chapter 7 describes the rewards and frustrations of sustainability work in law practice. Chapter 8, 9, and 10 explain and illustrate the use of systems leadership in three different aspects of sustainability law work: in client counseling (8), in making the law office more sustainable (9), and in the community (10). Finally, Chapter 11 addresses the future of sustainable development in law practice.

detail.abstract: An AI-service provider must decide which products to offer and how to price them. Customers buy products; backend policies determine how the service is delivered. We develop exact methods for choosing and pricing products under a product limit, and for jointly choosing products and the backend policies they share. Additional products have diminishing profit contributions before support costs, but sharing can make them cheaper to support together. Higher backend support costs can therefore favor more products using fewer policies. The central mechanism is a tension between demand-side substitution and infrastructure-side complementarity: products compete for customers, but can become cheaper to offer together when they reuse backend policies. In our measured application, four products selected from 400 backend-policy combinations capture nearly all the profit gain from using different backend policies for different tasks. Much of that catalog-expansion gain comes from task-specific backend alignment in the best single product, with additional gains from multi-tier screening. Broad measurement can support a small product line and an economical shared backend.

detail.abstract: Board oversight of artificial intelligence has been organized around capability: which models, which pilots, how fast to adopt. That framing is losing its usefulness. Powerful models are becoming widely available, and AI systems are moving from producing recommendations to taking actions inside enterprise systems. The questions that now decide whether AI creates value or accumulates hidden risk are questions of accountability. This paper proposes a practical framework for directors built on five dimensions: Value (where AI produces measurable economic results and who owns them), Context (the proprietary enterprise data, definitions and permissions that AI depends on), Authority (what has been delegated to AI agents and how that delegation is controlled), Workforce (how work, talent and career systems are redesigned), and Evidence (how the company knows its AI works and remains under control). Cybersecurity and operational resilience cut across all five. The paper connects the framework to the board's existing oversight duties, including the Delaware standard for mission-critical risk, and to the regulatory regimes now converging on AI. It gives particular attention to regulated industries such as medical technology, where the quality management system is becoming the natural control plane for AI. It closes with practical mechanics: committee placement, reporting cadence, a short board dashboard and an agenda for the first ninety days.

detail.abstract: Research assessment requires decisions about what constitutes contribution, which evidence supports that judgment, and how uncertainty should affect interpretation. Citation indicators provide useful summaries, but a new assessment system must establish the meaning and reliability of its own outputs. This working paper describes AIScore at the level of its public interface and logical architecture and proposes an independent evaluation protocol. It addresses a practical question: how can an assessment service be examined meaningfully when its scoring implementation remains proprietary? A purposive fourresearcher case series compares public Google Scholar indicators with AIScore outputs retrieved on 23 October 2026. Across the four cases, AIScore reported fewer global citations and lower or equal h-index values than Google Scholar, while also displaying publication-level scores and records-needing-review signals. These descriptive observations show why source coverage, identity resolution, and uncertainty flags must be evaluated separately; they do not establish accuracy, validity, or superiority over existing indicators. The evaluation protocol separates identity matching and metadata accuracy from score repeatability, agreement with independent expert judgments, sensitivity to incomplete evidence, and differences across research contexts. It also distinguishes replication of calculations from independent examination of observable behavior. AIScore is positioned as a prospective aid to evidence review. Claims about research quality, fair comparison across fields, or suitability for consequential institutional decisions require evidence beyond that reported here.

detail.abstract: For more than half a century, economic policy across sub-Saharan Africa, particularly in Ghana, has treated mineral wealth as the primary engine of national development. This paper asks why resource-led development has repeatedly underperformed human-capital-led development and argues that the answer lies in the structural limits of extractive dependence and the persistent underinvestment in people. Drawing on the resource curse literature and comparative evidence from eight economies across three continents—Ghana, Botswana, Nigeria, Morocco, Rwanda, and Kenya in Africa, and South Korea, Estonia, and India beyond it—the paper compares development pathways to assess why some economies have translated resources or scarcity into broad-based growth while others have not. It presents current data on Ghana's export concentration, the fiscal and ecological costs of unregulated mining, and the scale of opportunity represented by the global green and knowledge economies, which already sustain tens of millions of jobs and hundreds of billions of dollars in annual value with a fraction of the environmental footprint of extraction. The paper contributes a policy framework for governments and private investors to finance a rebalancing of national development strategy toward education, digital infrastructure, innovation financing, and green industry, without dismissing the legitimate near-term role of mineral revenue in national budgets. The argument is not that Africa should abandon its mineral endowments, but that it should stop treating them as a substitute for investment in its people.

detail.abstract: Firms often show warning signs before they fail. Before distress becomes visible, the way a firm finances its obligations commonly changes: profits stop turning into cash, debt service absorbs more of what operations generate, maturing debt is carried forward instead of repaid, and new borrowing fills the gap. This paper proposes six heuristic diagnostic constructs, comprising ten component measures, each examining one step of that chain: the Earnings-Cash Flow Divergence Index (ECDI), the Liquidity Exposure Coefficient (LEC), the Bailout Capital Efficiency Index (BCEI), the Refinancing Dependence Index (RDI), the Cumulative Cash-Debt Divergence Coefficient (CCC) and the Operating Core Debt-Service Ratio (OCDR). Every measure is defined from standard financial-statement items, with explicit rules for zero denominators and negative cash flows. The constructs are screening lenses. They indicate where to look; they do not establish misconduct, insolvency or causation, and no numerical thresholds are proposed. The paper positions the framework against the literature on accruals, distress prediction and rollover risk, gives a synthetic worked example, states falsifiable hypotheses with defined outcome variables, and sets out a validation programme. It reports no empirical results.

detail.abstract: Training program planning is an important part of human resource development to improve employee competencies and support the achievement of organizational goals. This chapter discusses various aspects of training program planning, including planning concepts, material preparation, selection of methods and facilitators, selection of media and facilities, and preparation of training schedules and budgets. Discussions are carried out through literature review from various relevant sources to explain the principles, components, and stages of systematic training planning. The preparation of materials needs to be adjusted to the needs of competencies and work standards, while the selection of methods and facilitators takes into account the training objectives, characteristics of participants, the availability of resources, and the competence of instructors. In addition, the use of appropriate media and facilities can support participants' understanding, both through direct and digital learning. Scheduling and budgeting also need to be planned in an integrated manner by paying attention to training needs, cost efficiency, availability of facilities, and evaluation of implementation results. Thus, the planning of a targeted and integrated training program is expected to increase the effectiveness of learning, reduce the competency gap, and support the improvement of organizational performance and productivity.

detail.abstract:
The global precious metals industry has developed sophisticated capabilities for refining, assaying, certifying, transporting and safeguarding physical gold. Established standards provide confidence in the metal's quality and market acceptability. Existing custody and clearing systems support important forms of ownership administration and settlement.

Yet the integrity of a physical asset, the legal recognition of its ownership, and the final discharge of an obligation through transfer of that asset remain distinct institutional functions.

This paper examines the interface between established gold production infrastructure and the requirements of independently verifiable, transferable and legally enforceable ownership.

It identifies the conditions under which physical gold can function not only as a traded commodity or investment holding, but also as the underlying asset in institutional settlement arrangements.

The GoldTech Ecosystem is presented as a proposed architectural framework connecting verified physical metal, custody responsibilities, evidence of legal title, transfer execution, collateral arrangements and settlement finality.

The analysis distinguishes existing market capabilities from proposed extensions and evaluates the legal, operational and institutional requirements for implementation across independent participants.

Particular attention is given to the strategic implications for refiners, custodians and precious metals institutions, including the difference between improved digital administration and expanded control over legally owned assets.

The central argument is that excellence in physical gold production and custody does not, by itself, establish a universally transferable and independently executable settlement architecture.

The next institutional question is not how to manufacture better gold, but how to make legally recognised ownership of existing gold more effectively transferable and usable.

detail.abstract:
Taxes, mortgages, pensions, rents and the voice of ordinary citizens all rest on one quiet assumption: that most people work for a living.
The Unneeded showed why AI and robotics may remove the need for much of that work, and why the change could arrive in a rush rather than a trickle. The Implosion asks what happens next, to everything that was built on top of wages.
Drawing on past shocks, from the closure of the coalfields to the collapse of East Germany, and on models calibrated to real national accounts and household surveys, it traces how the damage would travel: from jobs to tax revenue, from wages to mortgages, from homes to banks and insurers, and from towns to the state itself. It shows why the gains from cheap machines may flow to whoever owns the land, why most rich countries could lose 3 to 8 per cent of national income a year in taxes, and why a crash in house prices could hand homes to investors at fire-sale prices.
But collapse is not inevitable. Ian Kano sets out three roads out of the rubble, and what it would take to reach the one on which citizens own a real share of the machines and the land, before the window to build it closes.
The question is no longer whether the machines will do the work. It is what will be left standing once they do.

detail.abstract: Democratic societies and organizations alike strive for representation that reflects constituents’ genuine preferences. Yet, this ideal is undermined when voters make strategic rather than authentic choices. Voters’ decision-making is influenced by electability concerns, with individuals often selecting candidates they believe others will support rather than choosing who they truly prefer. This systematically disadvantages women, racial minorities, and other underrepresented group members. The current research provides the first causal evidence that ranked-choice voting reduces this strategic bias among everyday decision-makers, notably the bias working against underrepresented candidates. Across high-stakes election scenarios, including incentivized online elections and U.S. presidential primary election simulations, we find that ranked-choice voting reduces the influence of perceived electability on voting behavior, shifting votes toward candidates facing greater electability concerns. Relative to single-choice voting, ranked-choice voting aligns voters’ selections with their genuine preferences, yielding 2 to 7 percentage points greater vote share for underrepresented leaders in our studies. Our investigation demonstrates how voting system reforms can address a fundamental challenge in group decision-making: ensuring outcomes reflect true preferences rather than strategic calculations.

detail.abstract: A large share of AI/ML projects fail to progress from pilot to successful production deployment. detail.abstract: This literature-based review examines perceived organisational support (POS) and its relationship with employee well-being, engagement, and retention. POS refers to employees' general belief that their organisation values their contributions and cares about their well-being. The review draws on organisational support theory and social exchange theory to explain why fair treatment, supportive supervision, recognition, and favourable working conditions can influence employee attitudes and behaviour. It argues that support is credible when employees experience it consistently in everyday work and when policies are accessible rather than merely announced. The paper also considers limits: support cannot compensate indefinitely for unsafe conditions, excessive workloads, discrimination, or inadequate pay. Practical recommendations include improving supervisor capability, fairness, workload design, employee voice, and the measurement of well-being and turnover intentions. This is a synthesis of existing literature and reports no original empirical findings.

detail.abstract: This literature-based paper examines how organisational culture influences employee behaviour, workplace engagement, and long-term retention. It synthesises research on shared values, leadership signals, psychological safety, organisational justice, employee identification, and the employee experience. Rather than treating culture as a slogan or a set of formal values, the paper conceptualises it as the recurring pattern of assumptions and practices through which employees learn what is rewarded, tolerated, and discouraged. The review argues that culture affects retention indirectly as well as directly: it shapes the quality of daily work, the fairness of decisions, opportunities for voice, and the perceived fit between personal and organisational values. The paper also identifies important qualifications. Strong cultures can support coordination and belonging, but can become exclusionary when conformity is rewarded or dissent is penalised.
